title: What is personal space, and why does it matter?
examples: How close should I stand to people?
Should I ask before I hug someone?

explain.say: Imagine you have an invisible bubble all around your body. When someone steps inside it without asking, you might feel squished or uneasy. That bubble is your personal space. Look at the board: the bubble changes size!

draw.text: What is personal space, and why does it matter?

explain.say: See the smallest one? About 45 centimetres, roughly the length of your arm, is for close family and hugs. The next, up to about 120 centimetres, is for friends. Where would you stand to chat with a friend?

Look at the bigger ones: about 3 and a half metres for classmates and people we do not know well, and even more in a crowd. People like more space with people they know less. Can you stretch out your arm and feel your bubble?
Meet Kai. He loves hugging everyone! But look: Zoe leans away and looks uneasy. Leaning back or stepping away is body language that says, I need more space. What could Kai do?

faq.a: Personal space is the invisible bubble around your body that you like to keep free. Its size changes depending on who you are with.
asks: Tell me about the Close: family hugs

faq.q: How close should I stand to people?
faq.a: About one arm's length is good for friends and classmates. Watch their body: if they step back, give them more room.
asks: Tell me about the Personal: friends

faq.q: Should I ask before I hug someone?
faq.a: Yes. Ask: Can I give you a hug? Or offer a choice: hug, high five or wave? Everyone gets to decide about their own body.
asks: Tell me about the Kai asks

faq.q: How do I know if someone wants space?
faq.a: They might lean or step back, turn away, cross their arms, or look uneasy. When you see this, give them more room.
asks: Tell me about the Zoe steps back

faq.q: Is personal space the same everywhere?
faq.a: No. In some countries people stand closer when they talk, and in others they keep more distance. Watching others helps you fit in.
asks: Do people in other countries stand closer?

facts: Anthropologist Edward T. Hall described personal space zones: intimate up to about 45 cm, personal up to about 1.2 m, social up to about 3.6 m, and public beyond that.
A 2017 study of 42 countries by Agnieszka Sorokowska and colleagues found people in Argentina stood closest to strangers and people in Romania farthest away.

quiz.say: Your friend leans away when you come close. What should you do?
quiz.why: Leaning away is a sign they need more room.

wrong.0: Stepping closer makes them more uneasy.

quiz.say: Which zone is for close family and hugs?
quiz.why: The closest zone, up to about 45 centimetres, is for family and hugs.

wrong.1: That is the social zone, for classmates.
wrong.2: That is the public zone, for crowds.
